newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Discipline, foreign support aided Zaire's rebels.
newsitem.headline: Discipline, foreign support aided Zaire's rebels.

text.p: Discipline, foreign support and the collapse of President Mobutu Sese Seko's armed forces helped Laurent Kabila win one of Africa's fastest wars and seize Zaire in seven months.
Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo seized Kinshasa on Saturday after Mobutu fled because his generals said they could not guarantee his security.

Kabila has opposed Mobutu for three decades but his attempts to seize power in the 1960s and 1980s ended disastrously because he had too little support and Mobutu was able to call on foreign military intervention and mercenaries to put down insurrections.
But with the end of the Cold War and the emergence of friendly governments in neighbouring Angola, Uganda and Rwanda decisively changed the military balance in Kabila's favour.
Kabila's alliance was formed on October 8 last year and consists of four obscure political groups with Banyamulenge ethnic Tutsis as the cutting edge of revolt against Mobutu.

Western intelligence sources said neighbouring Uganda and Rwanda, seeking to neutralise hostile guerrilla groups operating from Zaire, threw their weight behind Kabila, covertly providing him with troops, training, logistical and diplomatic support.
Uganda and Rwanda publicly deny any direct involvement.

"Perhaps Mobutu's biggest mistake was to encourage these hostile groups to operate from his soil. By so doing he directly forced Uganda, but mainly Rwanda, to find a lasting formula and this came in Kabila's name," said a regional military analyst.
War started in eastern Zaire when the Banyamulenge, a community of roughly 400,000, resisted Zairean attempts to expel them to Rwanda, a land which they left up to 200 years ago.

But Kabila had been preparing for months before the Zairean army took on the Banyamulenge, and their fighters had a solid spine of veterans who fought with Rwanda's Tutsis from 1990 until they seized Rwanda in 1994 to end a genocide by Hutus.
The Western intelligence sources said the Rwandans threw in all they could spare into the fledgling rebellion in the east, and as the rebels gained ground Mobutu's foreign enemies joined up covertly.
Angola, for instance, gave air logistics and equipment, the sources said.
"Kabila's biggest success was to forge a domestic and international alliance ranged against Mobutu," said a Western diplomat in Lubumbashi, Zaire's second largest city.

Even far off governments in Eritrea and Ethiopia, which themselves had seized power in guerrilla wars as had Rwanda and Uganda, offered advice to Kabila because they viewed Mobutu as an agent of Western imperialism, the intelligence sources said.

As the rebel alliance gained ground and strength, Mobutu's armed forces collapsed. Troops, some unpaid for years and demoralised by no training and a command structure wrecked by corruption and tribalism, used the rebellion to loot and flee.
"We had no army worth talking about. All we had were reckless unpaid men in uniforms," said Kazadi Lupanga, a former officer in Mobutu's so-called "elite" presidential guard who joined the rebels.
Kabila was again aided by Zaire's rotten economy and political structure. Most people were disillusioned and rallied behind Kabila and provided much-needed intelligence about Mobutu's system.
"This was a local war and revolution supported by the people and helped by our foreign friends," said a top rebel official.

"Yes friends helped ... but we succeeded because of our determination, willpower, good leadership, a disciplined army and, of course, we must be grateful to Mobutu because he destroyed his structures so much that he could no longer be defended."
Kabila, stocky with a shaved head, is a former comrade-in -arms of the late Argentine-born revolutionary leader Ernesto "Che" Guevara, who fought in eastern Zaire in the early 1960s.
Guevara was initially impressed by Kabila but swiftly became disillusioned by him and his then ragged rebel band before they and the Cubans were defeated by foreign mercenaries in 1965.
Kabila told Reuters last week fighting the war against Mobutu, who ruled Zaire for 32 years, was far easier than the enormous challenge of rebuilding Africa's third largest country.

"The war was easy but rebuilding this destroyed and abused nation is the greatest challenge that I face. It is the biggest test for the alliance," said Kabila, who proclaimed himself president of the new Democratic Republic of Congo on Saturday.
